title: Reading the symbols in a methods section

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
A symbol in an equation stands for a quantity, and the paper fixes which quantity in words: in a clause beginning “where” after the equation, or in the sentences around it.

A subscript is a small letter or number set low after a symbol, and it is part of the symbol’s name. A subscript never multiplies.

Every term added to or subtracted from another, and each side of an equals sign, carries the same unit.

blocks.label: In plain terms
blocks.html:
Each symbol stands for a quantity, and the paper says which one, in words, somewhere near the equation. Often that sentence starts with the word “where”. Find it before you read the equation.

Two symbols side by side are multiplied: 2i is 2 times i. Papers also write times as × or *. They write “greater than” as >, so x > 0 says x is above zero.

f(x) is the output of a rule called f, not f times x (Book 0, C4). A letter before brackets can mean either. If the paper calls the letter a parameter, a fixed number, it multiplies. If the brackets hold the input, such as t, it is a rule’s output.

Subscripts. A subscript is a small letter or number set low after a symbol. It is part of the symbol’s name, and it does one of two jobs.

It can label. Hall and colleagues write E for energy and set a small I, O or S after it. E with I is energy intake (EI). E with O is energy output (EO). E with S is energy stored (ES).

For output this book writes energy expenditure (EE), the name Book 1 used. EE and Hall’s EO are the same quantity.

Or it can count. BW with a small i after it is the body weight in interval number i. BW with a small 0 is the weight at the start, the baseline.

This book writes a subscript on the line, straight after the symbol: EI, BWi, BW0. A letter or digit written after a symbol is a label. BW0 is the starting weight, not BW times 0.

So side by side means multiply, with exceptions. A name of several letters (EI, BW, UGE) is one name. Δ or d in front of a symbol is part of it. A subscript is a label. A rule name before brackets gives the rule’s output. The “where” clause tells you which.

Greek letters. They are letters like x and y, with names. Say the name out loud as you read.

letter its name say it what one paper in this book uses it for
ρ rho “roe” an energy density, energy per kilogram
Δ capital delta “delta” the change in whatever follows it
δ small delta “delta” a physical activity parameter: the energy cost of activity per kg of body weight (Polidori)
ε epsilon “ep-sih-lon” how expenditure depends on weight (Polidori)
Σ capital sigma “sigma” add up

Each paper decides what its letters mean, in its own “where” clause.

Sigma. Σ means “add up”. It comes with a counter, usually i, and the counter’s first and last values. On one line this book writes them in square brackets after it. Say the sum in words, then write it out.

Σ[i = 1 to 4] 2i
= the sum, for i from 1 to 4, of 2 times i
= 2 times 1 plus 2 times 2 plus 2 times 3 plus 2 times 4
= 2 plus 4 plus 6 plus 8
= 20

Units. Every term that is added or subtracted must carry the same unit, and so must the two sides of an equals sign (Book 0, B3). Use that to find the unit of a symbol the paper never states.

blocks.alt: Paired bars at i = 1, 2, 3 and 4. The first bar of each pair is 2, 4, 6 and 8 high; the second is 3, 6, 9 and 12 high.
blocks.caption: Two sigma sums drawn as their terms. The term for each i stands at i, so the counter only says where a term sits. The sum is the heights added up: 2 + 4 + 6 + 8 = 20 for Σ[i = 1 to 4] 2i, and 3 + 6 + 9 + 12 = 30 for Σ[i = 1 to 4] 3i.

blocks.label: Illustration
blocks.html:
Hall and colleagues (2012) wrote a consensus statement on energy balance — a text a panel of experts agreed on together. In it they write the energy balance equation like this.

ES = EI minus EO

ES is the energy stored in the body. The same paper puts the energy held in a lean adult’s fat cells at about 130,000 kcal. So the stores are well over 130,000 kcal, and the equation seems to say intake minus output is too.

Run the unit check before you believe that. The paragraph says what the terms are measured in: “All of these terms are expressed as energy per unit of time.” So EI and EO are in kilocalories a day.

The left side has to match. So ES here cannot be the stores. Their unit, kcal, has no time in it.

The paper says it in words: “ES is the rate of change in the body’s macronutrient stores.” The unit check caught the switch before the words did.

This book keeps the two apart. ES is the store, in kilocalories. Its rate of change is dES/dt, said “dee ES by dee t”. In this book’s letters Hall’s equation says this. The rate of change of stored energy equals energy intake minus energy expenditure.

dES/dt = EI minus EE

Polidori and colleagues (2016) worked out how much people’s eating changed during a trial of a drug. The drug raises urinary glucose excretion (UGE): the body loses glucose in the urine. Here is their Equation 1.

ΔEIi = ρ (dBWi/dt) + ε(BWi − BW0) + (Δδ/(1 − β)) BW0 + UGE

Do not read it left to right. Make a table with one row for each symbol. Fill the “words” column from the paper’s own sentences. Leave a cell empty rather than guess.

The words are in the Methods. “We calculated the changes in energy intake, ΔEI, for each subject”. One input was “the change of body weight versus baseline over each interval, (BWi − BW0)”. The other was “the rate of change of body weight over each interval, dBWi/dt”. That rate is an average over the whole interval, not a rate at one instant.

Then “The model parameter ρ was the effective energy density associated with the body weight change”. Here a parameter is a number the paper keeps the same for every person and every interval. (Book 0, D6 used the word for a number describing a whole population; papers use both senses.) Then “ε defined how energy expenditure depends on body weight”. And “Δδ represents changes in physical activity”. And “The parameter β accounts for the adaptation of energy expenditure during a diet perturbation”.

UGE is not spelled out beside the equation. When a short form is not spelled out, search the paper for words that fit its letters.

Start with the ones you know. The results give changes in intake in kilocalories a day, so ΔEIi is in kcal a day. Body weight is in kilograms. Time between weighings was counted in days, so dBWi/dt is in kilograms a day.

Every term on the right must also be in kcal a day. Work out each unknown unit from that.

ρ times (kg a day) = kcal a day, so ρ is in kcal per kg
ε times (kg) = kcal a day, so ε is in kcal a day per kg
1 minus β: a bare 1 can only lose a bare number, so β has no unit
Δδ times (kg) = kcal a day, so Δδ is in kcal a day per kg

That fits the paper’s words: activity has “an energy cost that is proportional to body weight”.

symbol say it the paper’s words unit
ΔEIi delta E I sub i change in energy intake, interval i kcal a day
BWi B W sub i body weight, interval i kg
BW0 B W sub zero body weight at baseline kg
dBWi/dt dee B W sub i by dee t rate of change of body weight, interval i kg a day
ρ rho effective energy density of the weight change kcal per kg (worked out)
ε epsilon how expenditure depends on weight kcal a day per kg (worked out)
Δδ delta delta change in physical activity kcal a day per kg (worked out)
β beta adaptation of expenditure to a diet change none (worked out)
UGE U G E energy lost in urinary glucose excretion kcal a day

Elsewhere the paper says urinary glucose excretion “was assumed to be ~90 g/day”, about 90 grams a day. Grams a day cannot be added to kcal a day. The paper says what the term holds: “UGE represents the energy losses”. Its Table 1 gives that loss as 360 kcal a day. It gives no energy per gram, so do not put 90 into this equation.

Now go the other way, from a written-out sum back to sigma. Take 3 plus 6 plus 9 plus 12. Each term is 3 times its place in the list, so it is Σ[i = 1 to 4] 3i. Check it by writing it out again.

3 times 1 plus 3 times 2 plus 3 times 3 plus 3 times 4 = 30
3 plus 6 plus 9 plus 12 = 30

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
The unit check shows that ES must be a rate in Hall’s equation.

The table tells you what each symbol denotes and what unit it must carry. It does not tell you that the model is a good description of anyone.

points.html: Find the “where” clause before you read an equation. Then write a table: each symbol, its words from the paper, and its unit.
One paper can use the same letters for two things. When the words are unclear, let the unit decide.
A subscript is part of a name and never multiplies. Read it as “B W sub zero”, out loud, until the habit holds.
Work out a unit the paper does not print from the terms beside it. Whatever is subtracted from a bare 1 has no unit.
A figure quoted in the text in one unit may enter the equation in another. Find the conversion before you put a number in.
Matching units show that an equation is not malformed. They never show it is right, and they cannot tell apart two quantities with the same unit.
Teach a trainee to read Σ aloud as “the sum, for i from 1 to n, of”. Then have them write out the first two terms and the last.

blocks.prompt:
Polidori and colleagues (2016) model the change in eating after weight loss with this equation, their Equation 4.

ΔEI(t) = − kP × ΔBW(t)

The sentence after it reads: “where the parameter kP>0 quantifies the feedback strength”. Their abstract reports eating “above baseline by ~100 kcal/day per kg of lost weight”.

Write the symbol table for Equation 4: each symbol, how you say it, what it denotes, and its unit. Then say in one sentence what the minus sign does, and what number kP took.
blocks.answer:
Go symbol by symbol.

symbol say it what it denotes unit
ΔEI(t) delta E I of t the change in energy intake from baseline, at time t kcal a day
t t time days
ΔBW(t) delta B W of t the change in body weight from baseline, at time t kg
kP k sub P the strength of the feedback, a number greater than zero kcal a day per kg

The (t) is function notation from Book 0, C4. ΔEI(t) is the change in intake at time t. It is not ΔEI times t.

The unit of kP comes from the unit check. The left side is in kcal a day. ΔBW(t) is in kg. So kP must be in kcal a day per kg.

The minus sign reverses the direction. Weight lost makes ΔBW(t) negative. Minus a positive kP times a negative number is positive, so intake rises above baseline when weight falls.

The abstract’s figure is kP, and its unit is exactly the one the check predicts: about 100 kcal a day per kg of lost weight. That is the paper’s rounded figure. The Results give the fitted value, 95.

a loss of 1 kg: ΔBW = -1
ΔEI = minus 100 times -1 = 100

About 100 kcal a day more eating for each kilogram lost, on this model and for the group average.

blocks.prompt:
Write this sum out term by term, then work it out.

Σ[i = 1 to 4] 3i
blocks.answer:
Put i = 1, 2, 3 and 4 into 3i in turn, then add.

3 times 1 plus 3 times 2 plus 3 times 3 plus 3 times 4
3 plus 6 plus 9 plus 12 = 30

The sum is 30.

blocks.prompt:
Write this sum in sigma notation.

2 plus 4 plus 6 plus 8 plus 10
blocks.answer:
Each term is 2 times its place in the list: the first is 2 times 1, the fifth is 2 times 5. So the counter runs from 1 to 5 and each term is 2i.

Σ[i = 1 to 5] 2i

Check by writing it out again.

2 times 1 plus 2 times 2 plus 2 times 3 plus 2 times 4 plus 2 times 5 = 30
2 plus 4 plus 6 plus 8 plus 10 = 30

blocks.prompt:
Four values are x1 = 4, x2 = 7, x3 = 1 and x4 = 8.

Work out Σ[i = 1 to 4] xi, then Σ[i = 2 to 3] xi, then Σ[i = 1 to 4] 5xi.
blocks.answer:
The first adds all four.

4 plus 7 plus 1 plus 8 = 20

The second starts at i = 2 and stops at i = 3, so it adds only x2 and x3.

7 plus 1 = 8

The third multiplies each value by 5 before adding.

5 times 4 plus 5 times 7 plus 5 times 1 plus 5 times 8
20 plus 35 plus 5 plus 40 = 100

That is 5 times the first sum, 5 times 20. A number that multiplies every term can be taken outside the sum.

blocks.prompt:
An equation reads A = B + C × D. B is in kilocalories a day. D is in kilograms.

Work out the unit of A and the unit of C.
blocks.answer:
A term added to B must carry B’s unit. So C × D is in kilocalories a day, and A, which equals the sum, is in kilocalories a day too.

C times kilograms gives kilocalories a day. So C is kilocalories a day divided by kilograms.

C = (kcal a day) divided by (kg)
= kcal a day per kg

A is in kcal a day, and C is in kcal a day per kg.

blocks.prompt:
Three United Nations bodies wrote a report on human energy requirements (2004). They are the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), the World Health Organization (WHO) and the United Nations University (UNU). The report divides total energy expenditure (TEE) by basal metabolic rate (BMR), both in megajoules a day. The result is the physical activity level (PAL).

PAL = TEE/BMR

The same passage gives a man with a PAL of 1.75 and a mean BMR of 7.10 MJ/day.

Work out his TEE. Then give the unit of PAL, and say why it has that unit.
blocks.answer:
Rearrange PAL = TEE/BMR for TEE by multiplying both sides by BMR (Book 0, C2).

TEE = PAL times BMR
1.75 times 7.10 = 12.425

12.425 MJ a day, which the report prints cut to 12.42.

Now the unit of PAL. It is TEE divided by BMR.

(MJ a day) divided by (MJ a day)

The two units cancel, so PAL has no unit. It says how many times the basal rate the day’s total is. A multiplier that turns one energy a day into another has to be a bare number.

blocks.prompt:
Hall (2008) writes: “The energy density of the body fat mass change, ρF = 39.5 MJ/kg”. He uses ΔF for the change in body fat.

Say both symbols in words. Then take ΔF = -3 kg, a made-up figure. Work out ρF times ΔF, with its unit, and say what the sign means.
blocks.answer:
ρF is “rho sub F”: the energy density of the body fat mass change, in megajoules per kilogram. The F labels which energy density, the one for fat. ΔF is “delta F”: the change in body fat, in kilograms.

39.5 times -3 = -118.5
(MJ per kg) times (kg) = MJ

Minus 118.5 megajoules. The kilograms cancel and leave energy.

The minus sign comes from ΔF. Fat fell by 3 kg, so the energy held in that fat fell by 118.5 megajoules.

blocks.prompt:
Polidori and colleagues (2016) define the length of each interval. They write “The interval length was t = (N−1)*T”. Then they say what the letters are. “N = 2 was the number of body weight measurements per interval”. And “T = 52 was the number of days between measurements”.

Say what t, N and T each stand for, with their units. Work out t. Then work out what t would be with three measurements per interval, the same distance apart.
blocks.answer:
N is a count of weighings in one interval, with no unit. T is the number of days between two weighings, so it is in days. t is the length of the interval, in days.

The asterisk is a times sign, as on a keyboard.

t = (N minus 1) times T
(2 minus 1) times 52 = 52

Each interval is 52 days long. Two weighings mark out one gap. Here t is a length of time, not a moment.

With three weighings there are two gaps.

(3 minus 1) times 52 = 104

104 days.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a worked answer. Find the step that broke.

Equation 1 of Polidori and colleagues ends in “+ UGE”
UGE was assumed to be about 90 g/day
so the last term adds 90 to the change in energy intake
the other terms come to 250 kcal a day for this interval
250 plus 90 = 340, so ΔEI is 340 kcal a day

The 250 is made up for this problem.
blocks.answer:
The third step broke. It puts 90 grams a day into a sum of kilocalories a day.

Every term in Equation 1 must carry the unit of the left side, kcal a day. A figure in grams of glucose a day is not yet an energy. It has to be an energy in kilocalories a day first.

So 340 is not a number of anything. It adds two quantities of different kinds. The right answer needs UGE as an energy, which the paper gives in its Table 1.

Why the wrong answer looks reasonable. The 90 is the paper’s own figure, and the addition is correct arithmetic. The unit was left off the third line, and a number with no unit beside it looks like any other number.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a worked answer. Find the step that broke.

one term of an equation is ε(BWi − BW0)
two symbols side by side are multiplied
so BW0 is BW times 0, which is 0
so the term is ε times BWi
with ε = 20 and BWi = 80, the term is 1600

Both numbers are made up for this problem.
blocks.answer:
The third step broke. BW0 is not BW times 0. The 0 is a subscript, part of the name. BW0 is body weight at baseline, the weight at the start.

The rule in the second line is right for most symbols side by side. A subscript is one of the exceptions.

The term is ε times the change in weight since baseline. For that you need BW0 as a weight. Say the baseline was 84 kg, a made-up figure.

80 minus 84 = -4
20 times -4 = -80

Minus 80, not 1600. The broken reading turned a change of 4 kg into a weight of 80 kg.

Why the wrong answer looks reasonable. It applies a rule you were right to learn, and every later line follows from the third. Written on the line, a subscript 0 looks like a number.

blocks.prompt:
A colleague reads Hall and colleagues’ (2012) equation and says this.

ES = EI − EO. The paper also says a lean adult’s fat cells hold about 130,000 kcal. So a lean adult has eaten 130,000 kcal more than they have spent.

Decide what to check, check it, and say what your answer does not establish.
blocks.answer:
What to check: whether ES in the equation is the store, which the colleague assumes. Use the unit check, and then the paper’s words.

The paper says of the terms: “All of these terms are expressed as energy per unit of time.”

EI minus EO: (kcal a day) minus (kcal a day) = kcal a day
the stores: kcal, with no time in the unit

The two sides cannot match if ES is the store. And the paper says so in words: “ES is the rate of change in the body’s macronutrient stores.”

So the equation says nothing directly about the 130,000 kcal. It says how fast the stores change on a given day. To reach a store from rates you would have to add up the daily differences over the whole of a life, from a starting store.

What this does not establish. It does not say the colleague’s conclusion is false. Stores do reflect intake minus expenditure added up over time. But it says the equation, read as written, is not the step that gets you there. It also says nothing about how the stores were built, or when.

blocks.prompt:
A trainee’s notes on two papers say this.

Hall (2008) gives ρ = 39.5 MJ/kg. Polidori and colleagues (2016) have a ρ in Equation 1. So in their model each kilogram of weight change carries 39.5 MJ. That is about 9,441 kcal.

Decide what to check, check it, and say what your answer does not establish.
blocks.answer:
What to check: the arithmetic, then the units, then whether the two ρ symbols are the same quantity.

The arithmetic first. A megajoule is 1,000 kilojoules, and 1 kcal is 4.184 kJ.

39.5 times 1,000 = 39,500
39,500 divided by 4.184 = 9,440.7

About 9,441 kcal. The sum is right.

The units. Both symbols are energy per kilogram, so the unit check passes. That is the trap: it cannot tell them apart.

The names. Hall’s symbol is ρF, rho sub F, “the energy density of the body fat mass change”. The subscript F says it is for fat alone. Polidori’s ρ has no subscript and is “the effective energy density associated with the body weight change”, all of it. Hall (2008) also reports Forbes’s point that “lean body mass is lost in concert with body fat during weight loss”. So a kilogram of weight change is not a kilogram of fat, and the two ρ symbols are different quantities.

What this does not establish. It does not give you Polidori’s value of ρ. That comes from their Equation 2, which needs quantities this section has not read. It shows only that 39.5 belongs to fat, and that the note borrowed it by matching a letter.
